forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Luton forecasts £2.83m overspend on £54.39m high needs budget for 2026/27
news_drafts.lead:
Luton Council's special educational needs budget is forecast to overspend by £2.83m in 2026/27, according to the first quarterly budget monitoring report (the in-year check of spending against budget) for the year. The report went to the council's Scrutiny Finance Review Group on 26 October 2026.

All of it falls in high needs, the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND). The allocation is £54.39m. The forecast already takes account of £0.88m moved into high needs from the Schools Block, a separate part of the schools grant, a transfer approved in January 2026.

The report says the forecast "continues to be driven by demand-led pressures". It also describes it as "subject to significant uncertainty". It says national SEND reforms have led to a "substantial increase" in requests for Education, Health and Care Needs Assessments, which are assessments of a child's needs for support. The report says these are expected to put further pressure on high needs and on related services paid for from the council's main General Fund budget.

news_drafts.headline: Luton procurement exemptions reach 680 in 2025/26, up from 321 in 2023/24, mostly children's services
news_drafts.lead:
Requests to bypass Luton Council's normal buying rules (exemptions to standing orders) rose to 680 in 2025/26, from 321 in 2023/24 and 566 the year before, the Audit & Governance Committee is told in its annual procurement report. The council approved 471 of them, with £41.8m in approved value.

Children, Families & Education accounted for 311 of the requests, 46% of the total. Its requests were worth £40.6m, 57% by value, and the council approved 244 of them (78%) and £21.4m of the value (53%). The report attributes the increase largely to residential care and foster care placements, out-of-borough school places for children with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND), and home-to-school transport. Rejections also rose, to 209 from 119 in 2023/24. About 44% were for administrative errors and 17% for missing conflict-of-interest declarations.

The council has set up a Passenger Transport Services Framework, a compliant route for buying home-to-school transport, which accounted for about £2.6m of exemption value in 2025/26. The paper says this is expected to "significantly reduce" future requests in that area. Members are asked to acknowledge that the council's processes, commissioning arrangements and procurement policies need further review for residential care, foster care and out-of-borough school placements.

The committee also has the first-quarter budget monitoring (the in-year check of spending against budget). Adult social care is forecasting a £1.7m overspend from demand and complexity, and the High Needs Block, the part of school funding for children with SEND, a £2.8m overspend even after an approved £880k transfer from the Schools Block. The corporate risks paper says the council balanced its 2026/27 budget without using reserves, helped by a 5% council tax rise and the government funding settlement, after a significant 2025/26 deficit that it did not size. It is pursuing a deficit recovery plan over two years.

On internal audit, of 349 recommendations followed up, 76% were fully implemented, 20% were in progress and 4% not yet started.

news_drafts.headline: Luton complaints handling falls short of 80% target despite quarterly improvement
news_drafts.lead: Luton's complaints performance reached 62.4% in-service-level agreement (in-SLA) in the year to March 2026, falling 17.6 percentage points short of the 80% target the council set for the first time in January. The council showed quarterly progress, rising from 60.8% in the first quarter to 65.5% in the fourth, and ombudsman compensation claims dropped 69% to £4,750. However, Children, Family & Education — the highest-risk area — saw complaints surge 54% to 216 while performance remained flat at 34.3% in-SLA, leaving cases unresolved at an average of 52.9 days against an 80% target. The council has committed to a dedicated recovery plan with weekly leadership review and targets of 60% in-SLA by the end of the second quarter and 75% by year-end, conditional on training completion and new platform implementation.
news_drafts.paper_title: 8 - Appendix 1 - Corporate Complaints Annual Performance Report (written) - 2026 v1.3

findings.headline: At the time of writing, the Council reports households in temporary accommodation at a record low.
findings.detail: The paper links this to a procurement policy review aimed at increasing the supply of temporary and interim accommodation, which followed a Housing Ombudsman service improvement order about a family placed in bed and breakfast for longer than permitted. It also states that no families are currently in bed and breakfast longer than permitted.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation numbers and the cost of placements are a major budget line for homelessness services, and a reported fall to a record low, with the procurement change behind it, is a result other councils would want to compare.
findings.figures: No figure for the number of households is given in the paper
findings.quote: At the time of writing households in temporary accommodation are at a record low and no families are residing in bed and breakfast accommodation longer than is permitted.

findings.headline: The lessons-learned field was not completed in 138 of 198 closed housing cases checked (69.7%).
findings.detail: The paper identifies this as a recording gap in the previous case management system, which it says would be a cause for concern on its own given the Ombudsman's emphasis on evidencing learning. It says the gap has been addressed in the new system introduced in September 2026.
findings.matters: Missing records of learning from complaints weaken the evidence trail an Ombudsman or auditor would expect, and the paper's move to a new system is a change other councils running similar case systems may face.
findings.figures: 138 of 198 closed cases (69.7%) with the lessons-learned field not completed
findings.quote: highlighted this field was not completed in 138 (69.7%) of cases.

findings.headline: 76.5% of housing complaints were responded to within the required timeframe in 2025/26, up from 61.8% in 2024/25.
findings.detail: The paper reports improvement at both stage one (75.3%, up from 62.5%) and stage two (82.1%, up from 58.8%). It notes that the response timescale was shortened to 10 working days at stage one and 20 at stage two from 2024/25, so the improvement was achieved against a tighter standard.
findings.matters: Improved timeliness against a shorter standard indicates better handling of complaints that carry Ombudsman exposure, and it is a result another council's governance team could benchmark against.
findings.figures: 76.5% (2025/26) against 61.8% (2024/25); stage one 75.3% against 62.5%; stage two 82.1% against 58.8%; corporate average 62.2%
findings.quote: There was a significant improvement in the percentage of complaints responded to on time with 76.5% being responded to within the required timeframe compared with 61.8% in 2024/25.

findings.headline: Delay in providing a service accounted for 53.1% of housing complaints in 2025/26, up from 27.5% in 2023/24.
findings.detail: Delay complaints rose from 102 in 2023/24 to 191 in 2025/26 at stage one. The paper says this trend requires further analysis and recommends identifying the specific services and root causes behind it.
findings.matters: A rising share of delay complaints points to service capacity pressure, which is the kind of operational strain that can translate into cost or backlog for a council.
findings.quote: In 2025/26 These accounted for 53.1% of all complaints received by Housing

findings.headline: Complaints about Building and Technical Services, which handles repairs and maintenance, rose from 56 in 2023/24 to 117 in 2025/26.
findings.detail: The paper reports that repairs and maintenance complaints now account for 26.9% of housing stage one complaints, against 13.4% in 2023/24. It describes this as a significant increase that requires further analysis, and makes a recommendation for it.
findings.matters: Growth in repairs complaints is a signal of rising repair demand or service pressure on the council's housing maintenance budget, and is a trend other councils managing ageing stock would track.
findings.figures: 56 (2023/24) to 117 (2025/26) complaints; repairs share of stage one complaints 13.4% (2023/24) to 26.9% (2025/26)
findings.quote: the data highlights that complaints relating to activity for which BTS is responsible have almost doubled since 2023/24.

daily_post.headline: The committee is asked to support a review of the Personal Travel Budget element, moving away from fixed bandings
daily_post.lead: Replacing fixed PTB bandings with individually set awards is a policy change that alters how a council controls the unit cost of SEND travel, which peers facing similar pressures would want to track.
